screens.title: Introduction to Unity Physics and Rigidbodies
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you will learn why Unity’s Rigidbody is the central piece of 3D physics and how it transforms a static object into a physically simulated one. We will explain the key properties that govern physical behavior — mass, drag, angular drag, use gravity, and the important Is Kinematic flag — and show practical examples where each property matters. You will see how a sphere can fall under gravity, how changing mass alters collisions, and how an initial impulse can launch an object. This chapter emphasizes common beginner mistakes, such as moving a dynamic Rigidbody by writing to its transform, and gives clear alternatives like AddForce and MovePosition. By the end you will understand when to use static colliders, dynamic Rigidbodies, and kinematic Rigidbodies, and you will be able to configure a simple scene where a sphere falls, then is launched using a script. Think of this chapter as the foundation for all interactive object motion in your games: mastering these settings leads to believable interactions and stable simulations. What will you build first with a Rigidbody?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Intro to Physics & Rigidbodies
Introduction to Unity Physics and Rigidbodies
How Rigidbodies make game objects behave like physical bodies

This short module defines the Rigidbody role in Unity's 3D physics system and previews the hands-on examples you'll build: a falling sphere and a launched projectile. Mastering these basics prevents common physics bugs and enables believable gameplay.

In this lesson
Add Rigidbodies, tune mass and drag, and apply impulses from C#.
Why it matters
Physics creates natural motion and reduces manual animation work for collisions and movement.
Visual concept
Static
No Rigidbody. Collidable but immovable — ideal for floors and walls.
Dynamic
Has Rigidbody. Responds to forces and gravity.
Kinematic
Moved by script, can push dynamics but not be pushed.
Explore Key Topics
Rigidbody Basics — What the component does and why it is required for physics.
Properties — Mass, Drag, Angular Drag and Use Gravity explained with effects.
Scripting Forces — Using AddForce and ForceMode.Impulse to launch objects.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will understand the Rigidbody component's role and be able to configure it for common use cases. First, you will identify when an object should be static, dynamic, or kinematic, and why each choice matters for collisions and performance. Second, you will tune physical properties such as mass, drag, angular drag, and the Use Gravity flag to shape object behavior. Third, you will apply initial forces in C# using Rigidbody methods like AddForce with the appropriate ForceMode and perform null checks to avoid runtime errors. Finally, you will recognize and avoid a common pitfall: moving a dynamic Rigidbody by setting transform. position in Update, which bypasses physics and creates instability. Each objective pairs a clear skill with practical reasoning so you know not only how to change a value but what gameplay effect it produces. You'll also get a short hands-on exercise to drop a sphere on a plane and launch it from a script, reinforcing these skills with observable results.

screens.title: What is a Rigidbody?
screens.narratorSegment: A Rigidbody is the component that tells Unity an object should be simulated by the physics engine. When you attach a Rigidbody to a GameObject it gains physical properties and becomes a dynamic object capable of responding to gravity, collisions, and externally applied forces. This matters because without a Rigidbody, colliders remain static: they can block or detect collisions but will not move under physics. Imagine a level floor and a rolling ball. The floor is best represented by a static collider. The rolling ball needs a Rigidbody so it accelerates, slows, and bounces in a realistic way. One practical example: adding a Rigidbody to a sphere at height five means it will fall to the plane automatically when the scene runs, following Unity's gravity. A common misconception is that colliders alone create physical motion. They do not. Colliders without Rigidbodies are efficient for static geometry but cannot react to forces. Another misunderstanding is to think Rigidbody equals animation; instead, Rigidbody provides simulation data you can read or influence. Key takeaway: attach a Rigidbody when you want simulated motion, and prefer colliders without Rigidbodies for static, performance-friendly geometry. Try this: add a Rigidbody to a crate and tweak mass to feel the difference in how easily it moves when pushed.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A Rigidbody enables Unity physics simulation for a GameObject, giving it mass, inertia, and response to forces.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › What is a Rigidbody?
Rigidbody — the physics body

Attach this component when you want the physics engine to control movement, collisions, and responses to forces. It gives the object mass and other properties.

Static collider: no Rigidbody. Efficient for immovable geometry.
Dynamic Rigidbody: simulated object affected by gravity and forces.
Kinematic Rigidbody: controlled by script, not physics forces.
Concrete example
Add a Rigidbody to a sphere at position Y=5. When you run the scene the sphere will fall and collide with the plane because it is now simulated.
Common mistake
Expecting colliders to move objects. Colliders alone block but do not move unless a Rigidbody is present.
Key Takeaway

Use Rigidbody to enable simulation; use static colliders for immovable level geometry.

Visual: Role comparison
Static Collider
Used for floors, walls; no Rigidbody attached.
Dynamic Rigidbody
Affected by gravity, forces, and collisions; use Rigidbody methods to move.
Kinematic Rigidbody
Controlled by the developer, still detects collisions but not moved by forces.

screens.title: Static vs Dynamic vs Kinematic
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between static, dynamic, and kinematic representations determines both behavior and performance. A static collider is a GameObject without a Rigidbody. It is ideal for level geometry such as floors and walls because it participates in collisions but does not move. Static colliders are computationally cheaper for repeated collisions with dynamic objects. A dynamic Rigidbody is a full physics participant: it is simulated every physics step, responds to gravity, receives forces, and both pushes and is pushed by other dynamic Rigidbodies. Use dynamic when you want realistic motion or physically correct collisions, for example a rolling boulder or a thrown crate. Kinematic Rigidbodies are a special hybrid. They are removed from simulation for forces and gravity but still report collisions. They are moved by script through transform changes or MovePosition and can push dynamic objects without being pushed themselves. Typical uses are moving platforms, doors, or scripted hazards. A common mistake is setting Is Kinematic on an object you expect to be pushed by players — kinematic objects will not be affected by dynamic forces. Make your choice based on whether the object must be simulated by physics, moved deterministically by code, or remain fixed for performance reasons.

keyIdea.title: Decision rule
keyIdea.text: Use static for fixed geometry, dynamic for simulated motion, and kinematic for script-driven movement that still interacts with dynamics.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Static vs Dynamic vs Kinematic
Comparison table
Static Collider
No Rigidbody, collidable, immovable. Use for floors and walls for better performance.
Dynamic Rigidbody
Responds to gravity and forces. Use for objects that should behave physically.
Kinematic Rigidbody
Script-driven movement, detects collisions, does not respond to forces.
Concrete scenario
A moving platform should be kinematic so it is positioned by code but still interacts with the player. A thrown rock should be dynamic to react naturally.
Common pitfalls & tips
  • Do not mix 2D and 3D physics components on the same GameObject.
  • Enabling Is Kinematic prevents being pushed by other Rigidbodies.
  • Static colliders should not be moved at runtime; treat them as true static geometry.
Pro tip

When performance matters, keep most world geometry static and only simulate what needs to move.

screens.title: Mass and Inertia
screens.narratorSegment: Mass is a core Rigidbody property measured in kilograms that determines how much force is required to change an object's velocity. In gameplay terms a higher mass makes an object feel heavier and resist acceleration; it also makes it exert greater force in collisions. For example, a heavy boulder with mass set high will be harder to push and will transfer more momentum when it collides with a lighter crate. This property interacts directly with applied force: the same impulse will accelerate a low mass object more than a high mass object. A common confusion is to treat mass like a speed limiter; it does not directly cap velocity but changes acceleration under applied force. When tuning gameplay, think in terms of inertia — how much the object resists changes in motion. In practice, set mass to approximate relative scale between objects, then adjust drag to control speed decay. Remember to test mass changes while the game runs to see collision outcomes and tune for satisfying feedback rather than physical accuracy alone. Mass and Inertia means mass controls inertia: heavier objects require more force to accelerate and influence collision outcomes strongly.. In practical terms, how mass affects movement and collisions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Mass and Inertia
Mass — how heavy an object behaves

Mass influences acceleration under force and the result of collisions. In gameplay tune mass to match relative object expectations rather than strict physics units.

Example
A boulder with high mass requires strong pushes and will impart high momentum to lighter objects it hits.
Misconception
Mass is not a speed clamp. It affects acceleration for given forces, not a direct velocity cap.
Key Takeaway

Set mass relative to other objects to create believable momentum and collision responses.

Tuning checklist
  • Adjust mass while the scene runs to observe collision outcomes.
  • Pair mass adjustments with drag changes to shape stopping behavior.
  • Use mass differences to communicate weight and solidity to players.
Quick scenario
If a crate seems too floaty, increase mass or apply less force on interaction to make it feel heavier.

screens.title: Drag and Angular Drag
screens.narratorSegment: Drag and angular drag are non-physical parameters Unity uses to simulate resistance, like air or water, without adding complex fluid dynamics. Drag affects linear motion, slowing an object as it moves. Angular drag affects rotation, helping spinning objects come to rest. Practically, you increase linear drag to reduce sliding or to make projectiles lose speed quickly. Increase angular drag when you want fast-stopping rotation so objects don't spin indefinitely. One helpful example: a thrown metal discus might have low linear drag but moderate angular drag so it flies far but stops rotating on the ground quickly. A common beginner approach is to set very high drag to stop motion abruptly; this can feel artificial. Instead, tune drag in small steps and pair it with mass adjustments. Use drag for broad damping; use physics materials and friction for surface interactions. Remember that drag acts continuously during simulation; it is not an instant brake. If motion feels jittery after changing drag, confirm you are applying forces in FixedUpdate and not manipulating transform directly, which can cause conflicts with the damping system. Drag and Angular Drag means use drag for linear damping and angular drag for rotational damping to shape motion decay and stability.. In practical terms, damping linear and rotational motion for stable behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use Drag for linear damping and Angular Drag for rotational damping to shape motion decay and stability.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Drag & Angular Drag
Linear Drag

Linear drag simulates air resistance and slows linear velocity over time. Use it to control how quickly an object loses speed after being pushed.

Example
Set drag higher for slow-moving projectiles or floating objects to make motion more controllable.
Angular Drag
Controls how rapidly rotational velocity decays. Higher values stop spin faster.
Common mistake

Using extremely high drag to fake stopping can feel unnatural. Combine moderate drag with mass tuning instead.

Tuning tips
  • Adjust values while the scene is running to observe continuous damping effects.
  • Lower drag for fast projectiles; increase for objects that should slow quickly.
  • Pair angular drag with constraints if you need to lock rotation on specific axes.
Analogy
Think of drag as wind resistance and angular drag as rotational friction that brakes spin.

screens.title: Use Gravity and Gravity Scale
screens.narratorSegment: Use Gravity is a toggle that determines whether a Rigidbody is influenced by Unity’s global gravity vector. In most projects the default gravity is a downward force that approximates Earth's gravity, but you can disable it per object for floating items or special effects. For example, unchecking Use Gravity on a hovering drone will prevent it from falling while allowing you to apply custom forces or scripted movement. This approach is also useful for objects you want to control entirely with code but still have collisions. A typical mistake is disabling gravity and then trying to rely on friction to keep an object in place; without gravity the contact forces change and the behavior may differ. Note that Rigidbody2D has a gravity scale property, but in 3D you generally rely on Use Gravity and custom forces. When you need different gravitational behavior between objects, disable Use Gravity and apply forces manually using AddForce to achieve finer, per-object control. Use Gravity and Gravity Scale means toggle use gravity to accept global gravity or disable it to control vertical behavior through scripting or forces.. In practical terms, control global gravity influence and object-level gravity behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Use Gravity
Use Gravity toggle

When enabled, the Rigidbody is pulled by the physics engine's global gravity. Disable it when you want custom vertical control or floating behavior.

Concrete example
Uncheck Use Gravity for a hover drone and apply upward forces selectively to simulate flight instead of falling.
Misconception
Disabling gravity does not automatically make position stable; you must manage vertical forces to hold an object in place.
Practical notes
  • Use gravity for most naturally falling objects for simplicity.
  • Disable it when you need controlled motion or custom gravity behavior per object.
  • Apply manual AddForce calls for bespoke gravitational effects or zero-gravity gameplay.

screens.title: Applying an Initial Force — Cannonball Example
screens.narratorSegment: Applying an initial force is a common way to make objects start moving at scene start or in response to an event. The provided Cannonball script demonstrates the pattern: cache the Rigidbody reference, perform a null check, then call AddForce with ForceMode. Impulse to create a one-time burst. First, always call GetComponent and test for null; if the Rigidbody is missing, log an error and avoid calling physics methods. Second, choose an appropriate force mode. ForceMode. Impulse is ideal for instant launches like a cannon firing. Third, multiply a direction vector by your force magnitude so magnitude and direction are both explicit. Example scenario: a cannon object launches a cannonball along its forward axis, using transform. forward times launchForce. A common misconception is using Update to apply physics forces that should be applied in FixedUpdate, which can cause inconsistent results. For a single launch in Start, AddForce in Start is acceptable because it happens once when physics initializes. The key takeaway is to use the Rigidbody A P I not Transform for physics-driven motion and to always validate component references before use.

keyIdea.title: Pattern
keyIdea.text: Cache Rigidbody, null-check, then use AddForce with the right ForceMode to apply instant impulses.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Cannonball Script
Code walkthrough
using UnityEngine;

public class Cannonball : MonoBehaviour
{
    public float launchForce = 100f; // Force to apply
    private Rigidbody rb; // Reference to the Rigidbody component

    void Start()
    {
        rb = GetComponent<Rigidbody>();
        if (rb == null)
        {
            Debug.LogError("Rigidbody component not found on this GameObject!", this);
            return;
        }

        rb.AddForce(transform.forward * launchForce, ForceMode.Impulse);
    }
}
Explanation & checklist
  • GetComponent<Rigidbody> caches the component and prevents repeated lookups.
  • Null-check prevents runtime exceptions and gives a helpful log if setup is missing.
  • ForceMode.Impulse applies a single instantaneous push suitable for launches.
Concrete example
A cannon with a forward-facing muzzle launches a cannonball with a single impulse, with magnitude set by launchForce.
Misconception

Applying continuous forces in Update can desynchronize physics; use FixedUpdate for repeated force application.

screens.title: SphereLauncher: Practical Launch Script
screens.narratorSegment: The SphereLauncher script demonstrates a practical pattern for applying an initial impulse with inspector-adjustable parameters. It exposes a launchForce and a launchDirection so designers can tweak behavior without editing code. In Start it caches the Rigidbody with GetComponent and disables the script if no Rigidbody is found to avoid runtime errors. The launchDirection is normalized to ensure force magnitude is consistent regardless of direction length. Then AddForce is called with ForceMode. Impulse to apply the instantaneous push. A hands-on tip: set launchDirection to Vector3. up for a jump, or Vector3. forward for a straight launch. Test values in the Inspector while the scene is not running; during play, changing them has no persistent effect unless you stop and re-edit in edit mode. Remember to attach this script to the same GameObject that has the Rigidbody. A common error is forgetting to normalize the direction, which makes forces inconsistent when the vector length changes. This script pattern is useful for spawn events, triggers that kick objects, and simple projectile launches. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

using UnityEngine;

public class SphereLauncher : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private float launchForce = 500f;
    [SerializeField] private Vector3 launchDirection = Vector3.forward;
    private Rigidbody rb;

    void Start()
    {
        rb = GetComponent<Rigidbody>();
        if (rb == null)
        {
            Debug.LogError("SphereLauncher requires a Rigidbody component!", this);
            enabled = false;
            return;
        }

        launchDirection = launchDirection.normalized;
        rb.AddForce(launchDirection * launchForce, ForceMode.Impulse);
        Debug.Log($"Launched sphere with force: {launchForce} in direction: {launchDirection}");
    }
}

using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerJump : MonoBehaviour
{
    public float jumpForce = 500f;

screens.narratorSegment: A reliable scripting pattern prevents runtime errors and inconsistent physics. First, get a reference with GetComponent in Start and immediately check for null. fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you will learn why Unity’s Rigidbody is the central piece of 3D physics and how it transforms a static object into a physically simulated one. We will explain the key properties that govern physical behavior — mass, drag, angular drag, use gravity, and the important Is Kinematic flag — and show practical examples where each property matters. You will see how a sphere can fall under gravity, how changing mass alters collisions, and how an initial impulse can launch an object. This chapter emphasizes common beginner mistakes, such as moving a dynamic Rigidbody by writing to its transform, and gives clear alternatives like AddForce and MovePosition. By the end you will understand when to use static colliders, dynamic Rigidbodies, and kinematic Rigidbodies, and you will be able to configure a simple scene where a sphere falls, then is launched using a script. Think of this chapter as the foundation for all interactive object motion in your games: mastering these settings leads to believable interactions and stable simulations. What will you build first with a Rigidbody?

By the end of this chapter you will understand the Rigidbody component's role and be able to configure it for common use cases. First, you will identify when an object should be static, dynamic, or kinematic, and why each choice matters for collisions and performance. Second, you will tune physical properties such as mass, drag, angular drag, and the Use Gravity flag to shape object behavior. Third, you will apply initial forces in C# using Rigidbody methods like AddForce with the appropriate ForceMode and perform null checks to avoid runtime errors. Finally, you will recognize and avoid a common pitfall: moving a dynamic Rigidbody by setting transform. position in Update, which bypasses physics and creates instability. Each objective pairs a clear skill with practical reasoning so you know not only how to change a value but what gameplay effect it produces. You'll also get a short hands-on exercise to drop a sphere on a plane and launch it from a script, reinforcing these skills with observable results.

This objectives slide focuses on applied practice. You will set up a simple 3D scene, add a plane and a sphere, and attach a Rigidbody to the sphere so it falls under gravity. During the live exercise you will adjust mass, drag, and angular drag to observe how each property changes motion and collision outcomes. Then you will attach a provided SphereLauncher script to apply an impulse and watch the effect. You'll learn to perform a safe GetComponent call with a runtime null check so your script disables itself if no Rigidbody is present. Finally, we'll practice toggling Use Gravity and Is Kinematic to see differences: disabling gravity makes an object float, while making a Rigidbody kinematic removes it from simulation but still allows collision detection. These tasks give you both the conceptual vocabulary and muscle memory for working with Unity physics in future gameplay systems.

A Rigidbody is the component that tells Unity an object should be simulated by the physics engine. When you attach a Rigidbody to a GameObject it gains physical properties and becomes a dynamic object capable of responding to gravity, collisions, and externally applied forces. This matters because without a Rigidbody, colliders remain static: they can block or detect collisions but will not move under physics. Imagine a level floor and a rolling ball. The floor is best represented by a static collider. The rolling ball needs a Rigidbody so it accelerates, slows, and bounces in a realistic way. One practical example: adding a Rigidbody to a sphere at height five means it will fall to the plane automatically when the scene runs, following Unity's gravity. A common misconception is that colliders alone create physical motion. They do not. Colliders without Rigidbodies are efficient for static geometry but cannot react to forces. Another misunderstanding is to think Rigidbody equals animation; instead, Rigidbody provides simulation data you can read or influence. Key takeaway: attach a Rigidbody when you want simulated motion, and prefer colliders without Rigidbodies for static, performance-friendly geometry. Try this: add a Rigidbody to a crate and tweak mass to feel the difference in how easily it moves when pushed.

Choosing between static, dynamic, and kinematic representations determines both behavior and performance. A static collider is a GameObject without a Rigidbody. It is ideal for level geometry such as floors and walls because it participates in collisions but does not move. Static colliders are computationally cheaper for repeated collisions with dynamic objects. A dynamic Rigidbody is a full physics participant: it is simulated every physics step, responds to gravity, receives forces, and both pushes and is pushed by other dynamic Rigidbodies. Use dynamic when you want realistic motion or physically correct collisions, for example a rolling boulder or a thrown crate. Kinematic Rigidbodies are a special hybrid. They are removed from simulation for forces and gravity but still report collisions. They are moved by script through transform changes or MovePosition and can push dynamic objects without being pushed themselves. Typical uses are moving platforms, doors, or scripted hazards. A common mistake is setting Is Kinematic on an object you expect to be pushed by players — kinematic objects will not be affected by dynamic forces. Make your choice based on whether the object must be simulated by physics, moved deterministically by code, or remain fixed for performance reasons.

Mass is a core Rigidbody property measured in kilograms that determines how much force is required to change an object's velocity. In gameplay terms a higher mass makes an object feel heavier and resist acceleration; it also makes it exert greater force in collisions. For example, a heavy boulder with mass set high will be harder to push and will transfer more momentum when it collides with a lighter crate. This property interacts directly with applied force: the same impulse will accelerate a low mass object more than a high mass object. A common confusion is to treat mass like a speed limiter; it does not directly cap velocity but changes acceleration under applied force. When tuning gameplay, think in terms of inertia — how much the object resists changes in motion. In practice, set mass to approximate relative scale between objects, then adjust drag to control speed decay. Remember to test mass changes while the game runs to see collision outcomes and tune for satisfying feedback rather than physical accuracy alone. Mass and Inertia means mass controls inertia: heavier objects require more force to accelerate and influence collision outcomes strongly.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Drag and angular drag are non-physical parameters Unity uses to simulate resistance, like air or water, without adding complex fluid dynamics. Drag affects linear motion, slowing an object as it moves. Angular drag affects rotation, helping spinning objects come to rest. Practically, you increase linear drag to reduce sliding or to make projectiles lose speed quickly. Increase angular drag when you want fast-stopping rotation so objects don't spin indefinitely. One helpful example: a thrown metal discus might have low linear drag but moderate angular drag so it flies far but stops rotating on the ground quickly. A reliable scripting pattern prevents runtime errors and inconsistent physics. First, get a reference with GetComponent in Start and immediately check for null. If the Rigidbody is missing, log an error and disable the script to avoid exceptions and unintended calls. Second, normalize direction vectors before multiplying by a force magnitude so the force applies consistently regardless of vector length. Third, select the right ForceMode: Impulse for instant pushes like launches and explosions, Force for continuous forces, and VelocityChange when you want to set velocity directly without mass influence. Fourth, consider the update context: single impulses are fine in Start or when triggered in response to input, but repeated physics operations belong in FixedUpdate to sync with the physics loop. Lastly, avoid mixing Transform writes and physics-based motion on the same Rigidbody; use MovePosition or Rigidbody methods for kinematic movement instead. Second, know your object types: static colliders are immovable and efficient, dynamic Rigidbodies are fully simulated, and kinematic Rigidbodies are driven by script and can push but not be pushed.
